title: HTML Is All Agents Need — James Russo, HeyGen
talk_summary: HeyGen's HyperFrames lets agents author videos as plain HTML/CSS/JS (LLMs' native training language) rather than a custom DSL, then renders deterministically by freezing the browser clock and seeking frame-by-frame. Their key lesson is that the thinnest wrapper plus a taste-focused skill beat heavy wrappers, and that small models are used as design partners to validate format choices.

takeaways.what_they_do: They tried JSON/XML DSLs and framework-specific wrappers, but the thinnest wrapper (plain HTML plus a few data attributes) produced the best agent output; skills teach taste, not the language.
takeaways.evidence_quote: the thinnest wrapper ultimately won, which is essentially just HTML at the end of the day with a few data attributes

takeaways.what_they_do: They validated format and skill design against a small cheap model (Gemini 3 Flash) on the assumption that if the small model can do it, larger models and coding agents certainly can.
takeaways.evidence_quote: starting with a very small model, Gemini 3 Flash, as our design partner

takeaways.what_they_do: Because models already know HTML/CSS/JS, their skill focuses only on what makes a good video (motion, narrative), and they continuously eval and use agents to improve the skill itself.
takeaways.evidence_quote: we don't have to teach them the language, we just teach them how to create good videos

takeaways.what_they_do: Browsers are async by design; for video they freeze the clock, seek to each frame, wait for all assets to load, screenshot, and repeat so output is reproducible.
takeaways.evidence_quote: freezing the clock and seeking frame by frame

takeaways.what_they_do: They note single prompts yield decent output but great output requires breaking the problem into pieces and iterating, with humans in the loop for last-mile edits.
takeaways.evidence_quote: Breaking the problem up into individual pieces and working iteratively
